pr_title: Fix NonBacktracking quadratic behavior with deep loops
pr_body:
This PR now actually fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/65271. The source of the problem was a behavior in NonBacktracking's derivative construction, where the rule for concatenations was causing quadratic rebuilding of concatenations. Abstractly, the rule for a concatenation `RT` (ignoring the case when `R` is nullable) is `d(RT) = d(R)T`. With just concatenation involved, this wouldn't be a problem, since NonBacktracking keeps concatenations in right associative form, so this rule wouldn't really recurse into itself. However, with an alternating nesting of concatenations and loops (as happens in the deep loops test), this rule ends up getting recursively applied and each time the concatenation `d(R)T` is constructed, the right associative form gets rebuilt, since the concatenation is to the right.

The change in this PR modifies the implementation of derivative construction to instead accumulate the `T` in that rule into a list that gets passed into recursive derivative construction calls. Then when the "leaf" of the recursion would have previously returned a derivative other than `Nothing`, it will now directly build the whole concatenation based on the "continuation" that has been already passed in. This avoids the quadratic rebuilding of the concatenations. The deep nesting of loops unit tests now finish in a few hundred milliseconds, somewhere between Interpreted and Compiled.

In the course of making this change I also got rid of an intermediate step of building a `TransitionRegex` tree for the derivative and then interpreting that for the current context in the input. I originally used it because I found it easier to reason with that as the intermediate step, but actually the derivative construction is more readable when done directly.

FYI, I expect outerloop will hit https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/65991.  Separately we should figure out what the right fix for that is.

There's a bug that these changes have produced, but which we'd have to deal with anyway when we get rid of the unordered `Or`. The bug is that the second phase of matching now is doing the "backtracking simulation", which is a problem with for example a pattern `(a|ba)c` on input "bac": the second reverse phase will follow the "ca" path and the "cab" path gets dropped due to the backtracking simulation. In general, I think the right thing to do is to just do the language theoretic derivative during the second phase.

I don't want to introduce yet another `_delta` array into the builder. Instead, I'm introducing a new node type `DisableBacktrackingSimulation`, which is metadata that the derivative creation function acts on. The pattern for the second phase will be wrapped in that. With this the reverse phase can still re-use the same `_delta` array. Let me know if anyone has any thoughts on this.

StressTestDeepNestingOfConcat, however, seems to have passed quickly in all variations on NonBacktracking.
I'll take a look at what the behavior for the new capturing mode is with patterns like this.

The source of the slowdown is interaction between the new captures-enabled derivative function `MkDerivativeWithEffects` and operations on the large `TransitionRegex` trees it creates. One problem was that new `Effect` kind nodes in the transition regexes didn't have a simplification rule for when the leaf regex is nothing `[]`, which was causing a blowup. With that the first step for that deeply nested loop goes through pretty fast. The second step then encounters some other source of blowup, which I'm tracking down now.

The second problem, and a more fundamental one, was that after the first character `MkDerivativeWithEffects` creates a `TransitionRegex` that has a leaf for each level of loop in the `(((...(a)*...)*)*)*` pattern to represent the different possibilities of which level actually loops again. Enumerating the transitions together with their effects was taking a long time. The backtracking matcher would just re-enter the innermost loop, so when traversing that `TransitionRegex` it is safe to ignore any leaves after the first nullable one. Doing this early exit does seem to fix the problem for this specific pattern.

I'll get this fix in. However, it is somewhat brittle, as when enumerating transitions it is only safe to check for unconditional nullability. A variant of that pattern with conditional nullability (anchors) in the mix could still hit this slow case. I'll discuss a further fix with @veanes .
